title: Bills of Exchange
description: Class 11 Accountancy: meaning and features of a bill of exchange, parties, promissory notes, accounting for retention, discounting, endorsement, dishonour, noting, renewal and retirement of a bill.

topics.title: Meaning, Features, Parties and Promissory Notes
topics.concept:
When goods are sold on credit, the seller may want a written, legally enforceable promise of payment on a future date. That instrument is a bill of exchange. The Negotiable Instruments Act defines it as "an instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer of the instrument."

Its features: it must be in writing, contain an unconditional order (not a request) to pay, be signed by the drawer, specify a certain sum and a certain date, and be accepted by the drawee.

There are three parties to a bill:

  • Drawer — the person who makes the bill and orders payment (the creditor/seller).
  • Drawee — the person on whom the bill is drawn and who accepts it to pay (the debtor/buyer). After acceptance the drawee is the acceptor.
  • Payee — the person who receives the money (often the drawer himself).

A close cousin is the promissory note — a written promise (not an order) by the maker to pay a certain sum to a certain person. The key differences: a bill contains an order and has three parties and needs acceptance; a promissory note contains a promise, has only two parties (maker and payee) and needs no acceptance. Two important dates also matter: the bill's tenure (its period) and its date of maturity = due date + 3 days of grace.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three parties to a bill of exchange.
examples.solution:
Three roles.

  • Drawer (makes it), drawee/acceptor (pays it), payee (receives money).

examples.problem: Example 2: State two differences between a bill of exchange and a promissory note.
examples.solution:
Order vs promise.

  • A bill contains an order; a promissory note contains a promise.
  • A bill has three parties and needs acceptance; a note has two parties and needs no acceptance.
examples.answer: A bill is an order with three parties needing acceptance; a promissory note is a promise with two parties needing no acceptance.

examples.problem: Example 3: A bill dated 1 March is for 3 months. What is its date of maturity?
examples.solution:
Add term + 3 days grace.

  • 3 months from 1 March = 1 June (due date 4 June after 3 days grace... actually due 1 June + 3 days).
  • Maturity = 1 June + 3 days grace = 4 June.

recap:
• Bill of exchange = written, unconditional order to pay a certain sum on a certain date, accepted by the drawee.
  • Parties: drawer (makes), drawee/acceptor (pays), payee (receives).
  • Promissory note = a promise, two parties, no acceptance. Maturity = due date + 3 days of grace.

quiz.q: A bill of exchange contains an unconditional:
quiz.explanation: A bill contains an unconditional order to pay.

quiz.q: Date of maturity = due date plus:
quiz.explanation: Three days of grace are added to fix the maturity date.

topics.title: Accounting for Retention, Discounting and Endorsement
topics.concept:
Once the drawer holds an accepted bill (a bill receivable), he can do one of four things with it. The accounting differs for each, but the acceptance entry is common: in the drawer's books, Bills Receivable A/c Dr / To Drawee; in the drawee's books, Drawer A/c Dr / To Bills Payable A/c.

  • 1. Retention till maturity — the drawer simply keeps the bill and collects cash on the due date: Cash/Bank A/c Dr / To Bills Receivable A/c.
  • 2. Discounting with a bank — the drawer needs money early, so he gets the bill discounted (the bank pays him the bill value minus a discounting charge). Entry: Bank A/c Dr (net) and Discounting Charges A/c Dr (the loss) / To Bills Receivable A/c. The discounting charge is the drawer's expense (interest for early money).
  • 3. Endorsement — the drawer transfers the bill to his own creditor in settlement of a debt: Creditor A/c Dr / To Bills Receivable A/c. The bill now belongs to the endorsee.
  • 4. Sending for collection — the drawer hands the bill to his bank to collect on his behalf near maturity.

In every case the drawee's books are unaffected by what the drawer does with the bill — the drawee still owes the same amount and pays whoever holds the bill at maturity. This is the elegance of a negotiable instrument: it can change hands freely, while the obligation to pay stays fixed on the acceptor.

examples.problem: Example 1: A drawer gets a Rs 10,000 bill discounted for Rs 9,700. What is the entry?
examples.solution:
Bank pays net; charge is a loss.

  • Bank A/c Dr 9,700.
  • Discounting Charges A/c Dr 300.
  • To Bills Receivable A/c 10,000.
examples.answer: Bank A/c Dr 9,700; Discounting Charges A/c Dr 300; To Bills Receivable A/c 10,000.

examples.problem: Example 2: The drawer endorses a bill to his creditor Mohan. What entry does the drawer pass?
examples.solution:
Settle Mohan with the bill.

  • Mohan A/c Dr / To Bills Receivable A/c.
examples.answer: Mohan A/c Dr; To Bills Receivable A/c (the bill is transferred to settle Mohan's account).

examples.problem: Example 3: Does discounting a bill change the drawee's (acceptor's) books?
examples.solution:
No.

  • The acceptor still owes the bill amount and pays the holder at maturity.
  • What the drawer does with the bill does not affect the drawee's books.
examples.answer: No — the drawee's obligation is unchanged; he pays whoever holds the bill at maturity.

recap:
• On acceptance: drawer — B/R A/c Dr / To Drawee; drawee — Drawer A/c Dr / To B/P A/c.
  • Drawer's options: retain (Cash Dr/To B/R), discount (Bank + Discounting Charges Dr / To B/R), endorse (Creditor Dr / To B/R), send for collection.
  • Whatever the drawer does, the drawee's books are unaffected.

quiz.q: Getting a bill discounted early with a bank gives the drawer cash equal to:
quiz.explanation: The bank pays the bill value less its discounting charge.

quiz.q: Transferring a bill to one's own creditor is called:
quiz.explanation: Endorsement transfers the bill to settle a creditor.

topics.title: Dishonour, Noting, Renewal and Retirement of a Bill
topics.concept:
Not every bill is paid smoothly. Several end-of-life events have set treatments.

  • Dishonour — the acceptor fails to pay at maturity. The earlier acceptance entry is reversed: in the holder's books, Drawee A/c Dr / To Bills Receivable (or Bank, if it had been discounted/endorsed). If the bill had been discounted, the drawer must repay the bank; if endorsed, he must settle the endorsee — and in turn the drawee again owes the drawer.
  • Noting charges — to obtain legal proof of dishonour, the bill is "noted" by a notary public for a small fee. These noting charges are borne ultimately by the acceptor (the defaulter), so they are added to the amount the drawee owes.
  • Renewal — if the acceptor cannot pay but wants more time, the old bill is cancelled and a new bill drawn for a further period. Because the drawer waits longer, he usually charges interest, which is added to the new bill (or paid in cash).
  • Retirement — the opposite case: the acceptor pays the bill before its due date. To reward this, the drawer allows a small rebate (discount), so the acceptor pays slightly less than the face value.

So a bill can be honoured, dishonoured, renewed or retired — each with a clear, logical entry that always preserves the basic truth: the acceptor owes a fixed sum, adjusted only for noting charges (added), interest on renewal (added) or a rebate on early retirement (deducted). With bills of exchange, credit trade gains a disciplined, enforceable backbone.

examples.problem: Example 1: A discounted bill of Rs 8,000 is dishonoured; noting charges Rs 100. How much does the drawee now owe the drawer?
examples.answer: Rs 8,100 (bill value Rs 8,000 plus noting charges Rs 100, which the acceptor bears).

examples.problem: Example 2: On renewal, who bears the interest and why?
examples.solution:
The acceptor, for extra time.

  • The acceptor asked for more time, so he bears the interest.
  • It is added to the new bill or paid in cash.
examples.answer: The acceptor (drawee), because he is getting extra time; the interest is added to the new bill or paid in cash.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is a rebate on retirement of a bill?
examples.solution:
Reward for early payment.

  • A discount allowed by the drawer when the acceptor pays before the due date.
examples.answer: A discount the drawer allows the acceptor for paying the bill before its maturity date.

recap:
• Dishonour: acceptor fails to pay → reverse the acceptance; if discounted/endorsed, the drawer settles the bank/endorsee and the drawee again owes him.
  • Noting charges: legal proof of dishonour, borne by the acceptor (added to what he owes).
  • Renewal: new bill for more time + interest (acceptor pays). Retirement: early payment + rebate (drawer allows).

quiz.q: Noting charges on a dishonoured bill are ultimately borne by the:
quiz.explanation: The defaulting acceptor bears the noting charges.

quiz.q: Paying a bill before its due date for a small discount is called:
quiz.explanation: Early payment for a rebate is retirement of a bill.

questions.q: A bill of exchange contains an unconditional:
questions.explanation: A bill contains an unconditional order to pay.

questions.q: The person who makes (draws) the bill is the:
questions.explanation: The drawer makes the bill and orders payment.

questions.q: The person who accepts the bill and pays it is the:
questions.explanation: The drawee accepts and pays — the acceptor.

questions.q: A promissory note contains a:
questions.explanation: A promissory note is a promise to pay.

questions.q: Date of maturity = due date plus:
questions.explanation: Three days of grace are added.

questions.q: In the drawer's books, on acceptance the entry is:
options: Bills Receivable A/c Dr; To Drawee
Bills Payable A/c Dr; To Drawer
questions.explanation: The drawer records a bill receivable against the drawee.

questions.q: Getting a bill discounted gives the drawer:
questions.explanation: The bank pays the value less its discounting charge.

questions.q: Discounting charges are the drawer's:
questions.explanation: The charge is interest for getting money early — an expense.

questions.q: Transferring a bill to one's creditor is:
questions.explanation: Endorsement transfers the bill to a creditor.

questions.q: What the drawer does with a bill affects the drawee's books:
questions.explanation: The drawee owes the same amount regardless of the holder.

questions.q: Failure of the acceptor to pay at maturity is:
questions.explanation: Non-payment at maturity is dishonour.

questions.q: Legal proof of dishonour is obtained by ____ the bill.
questions.explanation: Noting by a notary public records the dishonour.

questions.q: Noting charges are borne by the:
questions.explanation: The defaulting acceptor bears them.

questions.q: Drawing a fresh bill for more time is:
questions.explanation: A new bill for extra time is renewal (usually with interest).

questions.q: Paying a bill before its due date for a rebate is:
questions.explanation: Early payment for a rebate is retirement.

questions.q: A held a Rs 20,000 bill which he discounted at 12% p.a. for 3 months. The discounting charge and cash received are:
A discounted bill is dishonoured. The drawer must FIRST:
options: Repay the bank the bill amount (plus any noting charges)
questions.explanation: On dishonour of a discounted bill the bank reclaims the money from the drawer, who then recovers from the drawee.

questions.q: Why are noting charges added to the amount the acceptor owes rather than borne by the drawer?
options: The acceptor caused the dishonour, so he must bear the legal cost
questions.explanation: Noting charges arise only because the acceptor defaulted, so the cost is recovered from him.

questions.q: On renewal of a bill, interest of Rs 500 is charged and added to the new bill. In the drawer's books the interest is:
questions.explanation: The drawer earns interest for waiting longer, so Interest Account is credited (income).

questions.q: A bill for Rs 12,000 due on 1 August is retired on 1 July at 12% p.a. rebate. The rebate is:
questions.explanation: Rebate = 12,000 × 12% × 1/12 (one month early) = 120; the acceptor pays 11,880.

questions.q: A bill endorsed to a creditor is later dishonoured. The original drawer's position is that he:
options: Must pay the endorsee and can recover from the acceptor
questions.explanation: The drawer remains liable to the endorsee on dishonour and then recovers the amount from the defaulting acceptor.

questions.q: The maturity date of a 60-day bill dated 5 June (counting days, +3 grace) falls on about:
questions.explanation: 60 days from 5 June reaches 4 August; adding 3 days of grace gives 7 August.

questions.q: A key advantage of a bill of exchange over an ordinary book debt is that it:
options: Is a legally enforceable, transferable instrument with a fixed due date
questions.explanation: Acceptance creates a firm, datable, negotiable obligation that can be discounted or endorsed.

questions.q: When a bill is sent to the bank merely 'for collection', until it matures the drawer should:
options: Transfer it to a 'Bills sent for collection' account, still his asset
questions.explanation: Collection is not a sale of the bill; the drawer still owns it, so it is shown as a bill sent for collection.

questions.q: On the SAME transaction, 'Bills Receivable' in the drawer's books corresponds to ____ in the drawee's books.
questions.explanation: The drawer's bill receivable is the drawee's bill payable — two sides of the same accepted bill.
